title: Why Multi-Task SFT Fights Itself and Multi-Task RL Doesn't
hook: Train a model on several tasks with SFT and they interfere; with RL they coexist. The difference is a bound: SFT interference scales with gradient magnitude, RL's only with variance.
key_points: Under multi-stage training, SFT shows severe task conflict while RL keeps diverse tasks stable side by side.
At the parameter level, RL's updates across tasks are sparse and approximately orthogonal.
The theory: SFT interference is norm-limited, scaling with absolute gradient magnitude.
RL interference is variance-limited, bounded by the gradient variance that advantage normalization and on-policy sampling induce.
That small variance bound is what yields near-orthogonal optimization directions across tasks.
The authors use the insight to propose Parallel-RL, which decouples multi-task training for better efficiency and flexibility.
content_html: Anyone who has fine-tuned a model on several capabilities in sequence knows the pain: teach it the second task and it quietly forgets some of the first. Zhu and colleagues start from a sharper version of that observation — under multi-stage training, SFT suffers severe task conflict, while RL lets diverse tasks coexist — and go looking for why.
extra_html:
The parameter-level clue

Inspecting the updates, they find RL produces sparse, approximately orthogonal changes across tasks. Different tasks are moving largely different parameters, so there is little to collide over.

The bound that explains it

Their analysis of multi-task gradient interference gives the mechanism. SFT's interference is norm-limited: it scales with the absolute magnitude of the gradients, which in supervised training can be large. RL's interference is variance-limited: it is bounded by the gradient variance induced by advantage normalization and on-policy optimization, which is comparatively small. A small variance bound is exactly the condition under which optimization directions come out near-orthogonal — the geometric fact observed at the parameter level. From there the authors propose Parallel-RL, which decouples multi-task training rather than staging it, and report gains in training efficiency and flexibility.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

related.title: PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization
related.hook: Reinforcement learning is notoriously unstable. PPO's fix is simple: never let a single update move the policy too far. That restraint made it the field's workhorse.

related.title: FLAN: Instruction Tuning
related.hook: Teach a model to follow many tasks phrased as plain instructions, and it learns to follow instructions for tasks it never saw — zero-shot.

flashcards.prompt: What distinguishes multi-task interference under RL from interference under SFT, per this analysis?

choices.text: SFT's interference is bounded by gradient magnitude; RL's is bounded by gradient variance, which is much smaller
RL simply uses a smaller learning rate, so its updates overlap less
SFT trains all tasks simultaneously while RL always trains them one at a time

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper calls SFT interference norm-limited (it scales with absolute gradient magnitude) and RL interference variance-limited (bounded by the gradient variance that advantage normalization and on-policy optimization induce). The tighter variance bound is what makes RL's per-task directions near-orthogonal.

flashcards.prompt: What do RL's parameter updates across different tasks look like empirically?
flashcards.back_html: Sparse and approximately orthogonal — each task moves a largely different set of parameters, so tasks can coexist instead of overwriting each other the way multi-stage SFT does.

flashcards.prompt: What practical method did the authors derive from this observation?
flashcards.back_html: Parallel-RL — a paradigm that decouples multi-task training, since near-orthogonal per-task updates mean the tasks don't need to be trained in a single coupled stage.
